question: The 2025 Media Pluralism Monitor12 reports a medium-high level of risk to media pluralism for Italy, due to ownership concentration, lack of transparency and dependence on large online intermediaries. In the field of digital advertising, the top four operators hold more than 77 % of the market3.

The report notes that the Italian framework does not comply with Article 6 of the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA), which requires Member States to ensure full transparency of media ownership4. It also notes that national criteria do not include the protection of editorial independence required by Article 22 of the EMFA5.
Moreover, the Italian Parliamentary Oversight Committee on RAI is de facto paralysed, as those representing a majority do not provide the quorum required for meetings6.

Among the recommendations aimed at Italy, the report proposes: reforming the system of public support to the media in order to strengthen media independence, innovation and economic sustainability; ensuring fair and transparent agreements for the use of journalistic content by digital platforms; ensuring greater transparency of media ownership; and strengthening the independence of AGCOM, including through transparent appointment procedures.
In the light of the above: 1.
How will the Commission check Italy’s compliance with Articles 6 and 22 of the EMFA?
In order to promote independence and innovation, will the Commission support Member States in reforming public support systems for publishing?
What steps will the Commission take to ensure transparent and effective agreements between publishers and digital platforms?

European University Institute. https://cmpf.eui.eu/media-pluralism-monitor/. Italian Regulatory Authority for Communications (AGCOM), 2024. ‘Public access to information on beneficial owners remains very limited’. ‘Lack of a pluralism test that takes account of the independence of editorial teams’. answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.12.2025) The effective implementation of the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA)1 is a priority for the Commission. It is carrying out a dialogue with all Member States to make sure that their legal and institutional frameworks are aligned with the EMFA and facilitate its application at national level.

This dialogue concerns all relevant aspects of the EMFA, including the rules on media ownership transparency and media market concentrations. The responsibility for ensuring that the media sector can provide independent and pluralistic information while competing in open and efficient markets lies primarily with Member States.

EU State aid rules clarify the conditions under which public support may be granted by Member States, and the Commission has approved a significant number of aid schemes for the press sector. Moreover, through programmes such as Creative Europe2, the EU provides funding to foster media innovation and resilience.

Initiatives such as the Journalism Partnerships action3 (the yearly call for proposals is currently open) encourages media to collaborate and test business models to strengthen their financial independence.

Looking ahead, the Commission will reinforce financial support for journalism under the new Media Resilience Programme, which will bridge current support to media with the increased funding proposed in the new Multiannual Financial Framework. The Commission is monitoring the implementation of press publishers’ rights across the EU.

The effectiveness of the Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market4 will be assessed, taking into account market developments. The Commission is also monitoring under competition rules conducts from dominant platforms that might affect publishers.
